The Saptajana Hermitage

Stories from the Ramayana

The Saptajana Hermitage

The Penance of the Seven Sages, and a Forest Closed to All

In everyday English — Kishkindha Kanda, sarga 13

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read aloud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home and telling it to them.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little as you speak — Rama calm, Sugriva full of reverence, Lakshmana curious.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

At the end of every part is a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is from the Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sarga 13 — a tale of a single sarga, which happens on the road as Rama goes to Kishkindha. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — the young prince of Ayodhya. Tall, calm, kind. Warm dark-brown skin, black hair tied back, simple gold jewellery, a great bow decorated with gold in his hand. In the forest he walks barefoot, his upper cloth worn.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother. Like Rama, but a little shorter and lighter in colour. Bow in hand, simple green-beige forest dress, barefoot.

Sugriva — king of the vanaras, son of the Sun. Warm brown fur, royal bearing. He is showing the way — towards Kishkindha.

Hanuman — the powerful vanara, light golden-brown fur, long tail, gentle devoted face, saffron dhoti. Sugriva's most trusted minister.

Nala and Nila — vanara heroes, companions of Sugriva.

Tara — captain of the monkeys' captains, a greatly radiant vanara.

The Saptajana — the Seven Sages — seven great ascetics, who did penance for seven hundred years with heads hanging down, lying in water, living on air — and went to heaven with their bodies.

1 · Setting Out for Kishkindha · · SETTING OUT FOR KISHKINDHA

Rama had flicked Dundubhi's bones ten yojanas away with his big toe — and pierced seven sal trees with a single arrow. Sugriva's doubt was gone.

Now came the time — to challenge Vali.

Rama readied his great bow — decorated with gold, a splendid bow — and took arrows blazing like the sun, arrows that bring victory in war.

Then they set out from Mount Rishyamuka towards Kishkindha — towards the city ruled by the valour of Vali.

Sugriva led the way, showing the road. Behind him walked Rama and Lakshmana — and behind them came Hanuman, Nala, Nila, and Tara, the captain of the monkeys' captains.

This company — two princes and vanara heroes — walked together. Ahead lay Kishkindha, behind lay Rishyamuka — and between them lay the forest, full of its own beauty.

Pause and think — Rama readied his bow — decorated with gold, arrows like the sun. But was he preparing for war — or to help a friend? And Sugriva walked ahead, showing the way — does this show that the road is shown by the one who knows it? When you go to a new place, who shows you the way — the one who has been there before?

2 · The Beauty of the Road · · THE BEAUTY OF THE ROAD

As they went further, the road grew more beautiful.

The trees were bent with the burden of blooms — as if they were bowing to the travellers. Their branches were laden with flowers, and the fragrance of flowers spread through the air.

Rivers flowed — running towards the sea, their water sweet and clear. On their banks was green grass, and the sun's rays sparkled on the water.

The peaks of the mountains were high and beautiful — clouds rested on some, sunlight fell on others. The valleys were deep, the caves large — and everywhere there was a quietness, the forest's own quietness.

Rama saw all this — trees, rivers, mountains, valleys — and a peace settled in his heart. This forest was beautiful — but ahead another beauty was waiting for him, which Sugriva was about to tell him of.

Pause and think — The road was beautiful — flower-laden trees, flowing rivers, high mountains. Is the beauty of the road also a part of the journey — or does only the destination matter? And when you pass through a beautiful place, do you stop and look — or do you only walk on?

3 · The Hermitage of the Seven Sages · · THE HERMITAGE OF THE SEVEN SAGES

As they walked, Sugriva stopped — and pointed towards Rama.

Sugriva said: “Raghava, look — this is a spacious hermitage. Here are beautiful gardens, tasty roots and fruits, and sweet water — this hermitage removes the weariness of tired travellers.”

Rama looked — before him lay a great hermitage. All around were gardens — of flowers, of fruits. Fruits hung on the trees — sweet, delicious. And the water — clear, sweet, cool.

This hermitage was like a peaceful island in the middle of the forest — where a tired traveller could come and rest, eat fruit, drink water — and then walk on.

But this hermitage was not only beautiful — it was holy too. Sugriva said, “Rama, this is the hermitage of the Saptajana — of the Seven Sages. Hear their tale.”

Pause and think — Sugriva called the hermitage a ‘remover of weariness’ — gardens, fruit, water. Is a hermitage only a place to live — or is it also rest for tired people? And when you are tired, do you need such a place — where there is fruit, water, and peace?

4 · The Penance of the Seven Sages · · THE PENANCE OF THE SEVEN SAGES

Sugriva said, “Here lived seven sages — named Saptajana. They were dourly vowed — vows that no ordinary person could keep.”

Those sages lived with their heads hanging down and their legs up — as in shirshasana, the head-down posture — and always reclining in water. (Say this slowly — as if telling of a wonder.)

Their food was — air. And that too — once in seven days. Seven days would pass, and then once they would take air as their food.

And in this way — without moving, without eating or drinking — they did penance for seven hundred years.

Seven hundred years! For so long — heads down, lying in water, living on air — and then, when their penance was complete, they went to heaven with their bodies.

When Rama heard this, reverence for those sages rose in his heart. Such ascetics — who had conquered all the desires of the body — how great they must have been!

Pause and think — The seven sages did penance for seven hundred years — heads down, lying in water, living on air. Is this possible? And why would anyone do this — why give the body so much hardship? Does penance mean conquering the body, so that the mind can become still? And when they went to heaven — with their bodies — does that show that penance makes even the body divine?

5 · The Forest Closed to All · · THE FOREST CLOSED TO ALL

Sugriva went on — “Rama, by the power of the penance of these sages, this hermitage became like no other hermitage.”

Around the hermitage was a wall of trees — as if the trees themselves had formed a ring to guard the hermitage. Inside that wall no one could go — not even Indra, together with all the gods and demons.

Whichever bird or beast strayed into this forest by ignorance never returned. It stayed in the forest — as if the forest had taken it into itself.

From that forest rose a pleasing aroma — of flowers, of fruits, and of something divine. And sometimes — the jingling of ornaments, the sound of songs, and the music of wind instruments could be heard — as if unseen people were singing and playing there.

And above the hermitage — the smoke of the three sacred fires rose — Dakshinagni, Ahavaniya and Garhapatya. That smoke covered the treetops — and the treetops looked like gem-like mountain peaks covered by clouds.

Rama heard all this — and wonder rose in his heart. This forest — closed to all — was closed by the power of penance. No wall, no gate — only the power of penance.

Pause and think — This forest was closed even to Indra with the gods and demons — no wall, no gate, only the power of penance. Is power always visible? Or are there powers that work without being seen? And the birds and beasts that strayed into the forest by mistake never returned. Is that frightening — or does it show that there are places where, once you go, you do not wish to return?

6 · The Salutation · · THE SALUTATION

Sugriva said to Rama, “O Raghava, with Lakshmana, join your palms and offer salutations to the sages of the Saptajana.”

Sugriva said: “Whoever salutes these sages — no harm ever befalls them. Nothing inauspicious is ever seen in their body.”

Rama heard this — and joined his palms with Lakshmana. Both brothers offered salutations with reverence to those great sages — whom they had not even seen, but whose tale of penance they had heard.

Sugriva and the other vanaras also saluted — and then they all went on towards Kishkindha, well-pleased at heart.

After going a long way — they saw that city which could not be conquered by anyone — Kishkindha, ruled by Vali.

Rama and Lakshmana took up their sharp weapons — and with the vanaras, they went towards the city of Vali, son of Indra, to defeat the enemy.

Behind lay the Saptajana hermitage — peaceful, holy, closed. Ahead lay Kishkindha — where a battle was to come.

Pause and think — Rama saluted those sages — whom he had not even seen. Is a salutation offered only to people we have seen — or also to those whose tale we have heard? And Sugriva said — whoever salutes these sages, no harm ever befalls them. Is reverence also a protection — like armour?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

In this tale there is no battle — no demon, no curse. This is a tale of a road, a hermitage, and seven sages who did penance for seven hundred years.

Rama was going towards a battle — but on the way he stopped, he saw the hermitage, he heard the sages' tale, and he saluted. Does this show that even on the way to battle — one should stop for reverence?

Ask the listeners:

1. The seven sages did penance for seven hundred years — heads down, lying in water, living on air. Why would anyone do this? Does penance mean conquering the body?

2. That forest was closed even to Indra with the gods and demons — no wall, only the power of penance. Is power always visible?

3. The birds and beasts that strayed into the forest by mistake never returned. Is that frightening — or does it show that there are places where, once you go, you do not wish to return?

4. From the forest could be heard the jingling of ornaments, songs, and the music of wind instruments — but no one could be seen. Does this show that in holy places there is something that cannot be seen, but can be felt?

5. Rama saluted those sages — whom he had not even seen. Is a salutation offered only to people we have seen?

6. Rama was going towards a battle — but on the way he stopped and saluted. Even on the way to battle, should one stop for reverence?

7. The hermitage was a ‘remover of weariness’ — gardens, fruit, water. Is a holy place also rest for tired people?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book is from the Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, sarga 13 — the sighting of the Saptajana hermitage and the salutation, on the road to Kishkindha.

Setting Out for Kishkindha — Sarga 13

Rama readying his great bow decorated with gold, taking sun-like arrows, setting out from Rishyamuka for Kishkindha, Sugriva leading the way, Rama and Lakshmana following, and Hanuman, Nala, Nila and Tara coming behind them — this is at the beginning of sarga 13.

The Beauty of the Road — Sarga 13

Trees bent by the burden of blooms, the sweet water of rivers running to the sea, the high peaks of mountains, valleys, caves and caverned mountains — this is in sarga 13.

The Saptajana Hermitage — Sarga 13

Sugriva showing the hermitage — spacious, with beautiful gardens, tasty roots, fruits and water, a remover of the weariness of tired travellers — this is in sarga 13.

The Penance of the Seven Sages — Sarga 13

The seven sages named Saptajana, their dour vows, lying in water with heads down and legs up, taking air as food once in seven nights, doing penance for seven hundred years and going to heaven with their bodies — this is in sarga 13.

The Forest Closed to All — Sarga 13

The hermitage walled by trees, unassailable even for Indra together with the gods and demons, the bird or beast that strays in by ignorance never returning, the fragrance, the jingling of ornaments, songs and wind instruments, and the smoke of the three sacred fires covering the treetops like gem-like mountain peaks covered by clouds — this is in sarga 13.

The Salutation — Sarga 13

Sugriva asking Rama and Lakshmana to salute the Saptajana sages with folded palms, ‘whoever salutes these sages, no harm ever befalls them’, Rama and Lakshmana saluting, and going on well-pleased to see Kishkindha from afar — this is at the end of sarga 13.

The Three Sacred Fires

Dakshinagni, Ahavaniya and Garhapatya — these are the three sacred fires of the Vedic sacrifice, which burned without ceasing in a hermitage.

What Happens Next

In Kishkindha, Sugriva will challenge Vali — and Rama, hidden, will strike Vali with an arrow. That tale is in the next books of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here the tale of the Saptajana hermitage comes to rest — a road, a hermitage, and seven sages who did penance for seven hundred years with heads down, lying in water, living on air — and went to heaven with their bodies.

And whenever you pass a holy place — stop, join your palms, and salute. As Rama did — to sages whom he had not even seen.

— The End —
